title: Our First Winter Living in a Van (No Hookups)
creator: Wren Callaway
description:
Six weeks of snow, one van, two people and a dog. What worked, what froze, and what we'd change.

sentences.t: It's minus twelve outside, there's about a foot of fresh snow on the roof, and inside the van it's a toasty nineteen degrees.
We've been living in here through the winter for six weeks now, and a lot of you asked how that's even possible with no campground hookups.
So today I'm going to walk you through everything, what's worked, what's frozen, and the one night we almost gave up and got a hotel.
Let's start with the boring but important stuff, insulation.
When we built the van, we put wool insulation in the walls and the ceiling, and closed cell foam under the floor.
At the time it felt like overkill for a van we mostly used in summer.
Now I'm extremely grateful past us did that.
The windows were the weak spot, though.
The cab windows especially just pour cold air into the van at night.
So we made these insulated window covers out of reflective foam and black fabric, and they snap in with little magnets.
They are ugly, they are amazing, and they made a bigger difference than anything else we did.
Next is heat.
We have a small diesel heater mounted under the passenger seat, and it pulls fuel straight from the van's tank.
It uses a tiny amount of diesel, something like a liter every ten hours on low, and it keeps the van warm all night.
We also carry a little backup propane heater, but honestly we've only turned it on once, during a fuel line hiccup.
The big enemy in winter isn't actually the cold, it's condensation.
Two people and a dog breathing all night in a small metal box produces a shocking amount of moisture.
Our dog, Pepper, doesn't help, because she sleeps right up against the window and breathes on it all night.
On our first cold night, we woke up to water literally dripping off the ceiling onto our faces.
The fix was ventilation, even when it feels wrong.
We crack the roof fan open about an inch all night, and we run a little dehumidifier during the day.
Water was the next problem.
Our fresh water tank is inside the van, so that's fine, but the drain line runs underneath, and it froze solid on night three.
Now we keep a bucket under the sink and empty it every morning, which isn't glamorous, but it works.
And we fill our water jugs at gas stations and grocery stores, which means we've gotten very good at asking strangers if we can use their tap.
Now, have you ever wondered how we keep the fridge, the heater fan, the lights, and two laptops running out here, with no hookup and almost no sun?
The answer is a Voltera power station, and they're the sponsor of today's video, which made me very happy, because we were already using one.
This is the Voltera Base 2, and it sits right here under the bench, wired into the van's twelve volt system.
It's a lithium iron phosphate battery, which means it can be charged and discharged thousands of times without wearing out, and it's way safer than older lithium batteries.
That matters a lot when the battery lives a few feet from where you sleep.
It stores just over two kilowatt hours, which for us is about two full days of normal use without charging at all.
And there are enough outlets on the front for everything, four regular plugs, a couple of fast-charging USB-C ports, and a car-style socket for the fridge.
And in winter, charging is the real challenge.
Our solar panels are covered in snow half the time, and even when they're clear, the days are so short we're lucky to get a third of our summer input.
So the feature that saved us is that the Voltera can charge from the van's alternator while we drive.
An hour of driving puts back most of what we use in a day, so on cloudy weeks, we plan a short drive into town for groceries and that tops us up.
It can also take wall power, so if we stop at a friend's house or a cafe with an outlet, it charges from empty to full in about an hour and a half.
You can also chain an extra battery onto it later, which is what we're planning to do before next winter, so you're never stuck with the size you started with.
The other thing I love is the app.
I can check the battery level from bed, see exactly how much the fridge and the heater fan are pulling, and get a warning if something is drawing more than it should.
That actually caught a problem for us, when our water pump's switch got stuck and it was running all night, and I got a notification at two in the morning.
Annoying, but much better than waking up to a dead battery in a snowstorm.
It works fine in the cold, too, as long as it's inside the heated space, and it has a built-in heater for the battery cells so it can charge safely below freezing.
It's also quiet, with no fan noise at night, which matters a lot when your bedroom is also your living room and your kitchen.
It comes with a five year warranty, which was a big deal for us, because this is the one piece of gear in the van we really can't live without.
We've had ours for a little over a year now, through a whole summer of solar and now this winter, and it hasn't missed a beat.
If you're building a van, or you just want backup power for your house when the grid goes down, I genuinely think this is the one to get.
Voltera is giving our viewers a hundred and fifty dollars off the Base 2 with code WREN at voltera.com slash wren.
That's voltera.com slash wren, code WREN, and it's linked first thing in the description.
Thanks so much to Voltera for supporting what we do out here.
So, cooking in winter.
We cook on a single induction plate, which runs off the battery, and in summer we cook outside a lot, but in winter everything happens inside.
That means more condensation, so the roof fan goes up to full whenever a pot is boiling.
Our winter go-to is a big pot of lentil soup that lasts us two or three days, because nobody wants to do dishes with half-frozen water.
Okay, the night we almost gave up.
About three weeks in, a storm came through with winds over eighty kilometers an hour, and the whole van was rocking side to side.
The dog was terrified, I was terrified, and at one point a branch came down right next to us.
We moved the van at midnight to a sheltered spot behind a grocery store, and we sat there with tea, not sleeping, until the wind died down at five.
And in the morning, the sun came up over the snow and it was the most beautiful thing I've ever seen, so, we stayed.
Would we do another winter?
Yes, but we'd change a few things.
We'd add a second roof vent, we'd insulate the drain line properly, and we'd get proper snow tires before the first storm instead of after.
If you're thinking about winter van life, start with short trips, and learn what fails before you're far from help.
Next week we're heading north to try and see the northern lights, so stay tuned for that.
Thanks for watching, and stay warm out there.
